Findings: When round-tripping a vector of 100,000 random numbers through Julia and back (JuliaCall("identity", ...) / jlcall("identity",
...)), JuliaExcel's returned values matched the input exactly every time. JuliaInXL's did not: 17 of the 100,000 values (0.017%)
Each difference is exactly a power of two, one ULP ("unit in the last place") at that value's magnitude — the most common
being 2^-54. This pattern is the signature of numbers passing through a decimal-text representation with slightly too few
significant digits: most doubles round-trip exactly with 15–16 digits, but a minority need the full 17, and a fixed-width format
that provides only 15 would corrupt just that minority by a bit or two.
We can't confirm the exact mechanism, since JuliaInXL's Excel-side component is closed source, but a plausible contributor is
that .NET's default double-to-text conversion used 15 significant digits before .NET Core 3.0 (2019) — a runtime old enough to
plausibly predate JuliaInXL's own last update.
